cim: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"
kihagyva: P3: 40 pont, tendencia 20%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence is expected to be the biggest driver of change in academic research, according to 83% of academic librarians surveyed in a new global study from Elsevier. However, 81% also identify the misuse of AI as the greatest threat to the integrity of the scholarly record.

The findings come from Elsevier’s Librarian of the Future report, which draws on responses from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders.

The research highlights the increasingly strategic role librarians could play within universities as institutions respond to technological change, evolving research needs and growing concerns around research integrity.

Almost all respondents (95%) expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years, while 82% believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers. More than three-quarters (76%) also believe librarians should contribute to AI governance.

Despite these expectations, only 30% report that their institution has implemented an AI policy, suggesting a significant gap between the adoption of AI technologies and the development of institutional frameworks to manage their use.

Ann Gabriel, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Networks at Elsevier, said: “Librarians have always been essential to research, but this study shows an opportunity for their expertise to play an even more strategic role. As AI transforms how research is discovered, conducted and evaluated, librarians bring a unique combination of technical expertise, ethical judgement and trusted relationships across their institutions. Ensuring they have the skills, support and visibility to contribute fully will be important as universities navigate this next phase of change.”

The report suggests that librarians are increasingly positioning themselves as partners in the wider research process, rather than solely as providers of information resources. Alongside AI literacy and governance, demand is expected to grow for library expertise in open access, research data management and research integrity.

More than three-quarters of respondents (76%) anticipate greater collaboration between libraries and other university departments over the next five years.

The findings also point to the growing importance of leadership, influencing skills and the ability to navigate complex institutional decisions as librarians take on broader responsibilities.

Jim O’Donnell, University Librarian and Professor at Arizona State University, said: “Librarians long thought we were in the book business, or perhaps the information business. This survey shows that the community now broadly recognises we’re in the research business, working with researchers and learners in fresh and different ways, with exhilarating possibilities ahead of us. The onrush of AI offers us a remarkable opportunity to become our best selves in a rapidly changing environment.”

Taken together, the findings suggest that AI could provide an opportunity for academic libraries to strengthen their influence over institutional research strategy.

However, the contrast between librarians’ willingness to contribute to AI governance and the relatively low proportion of institutions with established AI policies raises questions about whether universities are sufficiently prepared to make use of that expertise.

The report identifies responsible AI adoption, trusted information and research integrity as areas in which librarians could play a more prominent role in supporting researchers and institutional leadership.

Elsevier says it will continue working with the global library community to explore how the profession can respond to these changing demands. The full report is available at Librarian of the Future.
